content.title: How To Watch Atremis II's Orion Capsule Splashdown On Streaming
content.text: IN SPACE - APRIL 04: In this handout image provided by NASA, NASA astronaut and Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch peers out of one of the Orion spacecraft's main cabin windows, looking back at Earth, as the crew travels towards the Moon on April 4, 2026. NASA's Artemis II mission will take Wiseman, Glover, Koch, and Hansen on a 10-day journey around the Moon and back aboard their Orion spacecraft. (Photo by NASA via Getty Images)NASA via Getty ImagesNASA’s Artemis II mission to the moon concludes on Friday when the Orion spacecraft returns to Earth and splashes down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego.The Artemis II mission began on April 1 when NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman (commander), Victor Glover (pilot) and Christina Koch (mission specialist), joined by Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, achieved liftoff aboard NASA’s heavy-lift rocket, the SLS (Space Launch System), from Launch Pad 39-B at Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Fla.ForbesNASA’s New Moon Base Plan Explains Why It’s Going Back To The MoonThe objective of the first crewed Artemis flight was to mark “a key step toward long‑term return to the Moon and future missions to Mars,” according to NASA.gov. While aboard the Orion spacecraft Integrity, the Artemis II crew ventured around the moon, and in the process, Wiseman, Glover, Koch and Hansen flew farther away from Earth than any humans in history at a distance of 252,757 miles.CAPE CANAVERAL, FLORIDA - APRIL 01: (L-R) Mission specialist Jeremy Hansen of CSA (Canadian Space Agency), pilot Victor Glover, mission specialist Christina Koch and commander Reid Wiseman walk out of the Neil A. Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building ahead of the launch of the Artemis II at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center on April 01, 2026 in Cape Canaveral, Florida. The 322-foot-tall Artemis II Space Launch System rocket and Orion spacecraft will take the astronauts around the moon and back, 230,000 miles out into space and the farthest any human has ever traveled from Earth. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)Getty ImagesWhile the Artemis II mission didn’t involve a moon landing — it did pass within 4,070 miles of the lunar surface — it was still very eventful, as the astronauts experienced, among other things, an Earthrise, Earthset and a total solar eclipse during their lunar flyby.The Artemis II space mission will conclude much in way NASA’s Apollo moon missions did more than 50 years ago, as the Orion spacecraft capsule carrying the crew will return to Earth with the aid of parachutes. Per NASA, the Artemis II crew will splash down in the Pacific Ocean at approximately 8:07 p.m. ET/5:07 p.m. PT. ForbesNASA Sets 2028 Launch For First Nuclear Mission To Mars Days Before Return To The MoonBy Jamie Carter“Following splashdown, recovery teams will retrieve the crew using helicopters and deliver them to the USS John P. Murtha,” according to NASA.gov. “Once aboard, the astronauts will undergo post-mission medical evaluations in the ship’s medical bay before traveling back to shore to meet with an aircraft bound for NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.”Where You Can Watch The Artemis II SplashdownThe Artemis II splashdown will be available on several streaming platforms online, including NASA’s YouTube channel in the embedded video above. In addition, the online platforms NASA+, Amazon Prime Video, Apple TV, Hulu, Netflix, HBO Max and Roku will also be streaming the splashdown.The Artemis II splashdown is sure to attract a large viewing audience, as the mission’s launch did on April 1. The Artemis II launch, which streamed on NASA’s YouTube channel — and was broadcast live on ABC, CBS, NBC, Telemundo, CNN, FOX News Channel and MS NOW — attracted 18.1 million viewers, according to Nielsen (via The Wrap). The rating was measured during the launch period from approximately 6 to 6:30 p.m. ET/3 to 3:30 p.m. PT.ForbesArtemis II Is Rekindling Hope During Humanity’s Darkest TimesBy Joe Sills
